items.abstract: Abstract Mindfulness has become increasingly embedded in organizational and professional settings, where it is often promoted as a way to enhance well-being and productivity. Drawing on Critical Race Theory, this study interrogates this claim by examining how diversity, equity, and inclusion are experienced within mindfulness communities of practice. Based on 31 in-depth interviews with mindfulness practitioners, instructors, and organizational leaders, we show that racialized individuals actively negotiate safety and belonging when engaging with mindfulness communities. Our findings reveal that safety and belonging are undermined by two process mechanisms: universalism , which frames mindfulness as a practice that benefits all humanity, obscuring the systemic inequities that shape its impact; and commodification , in which the commercialization of mindfulness leads to differential access to resources and pressure to conform to norms that disproportionately affect practitioners of color. Across individual, group, leader, and societal levels, these dynamics determine who can participate safely and belong fully, suggesting that it is not solely the mindfulness container that drives these experiences as outcomes but also the surrounding reified power structures. This research contributes to business ethics scholarship by highlighting how well-intentioned organizational practices can reproduce inequality and exclusion when broader social structures and power relations remain unaddressed, placing the burden onto individual practitioners.
items.title: The Consequences of Universalism and Commodification in Contemporary Mindfulness Communities: A Critical Race Theory Perspective

items.abstract: Due to the urgent need for planet-saving actions, calls to engage in sufficiency-based business practices are becoming more widespread. Drawing on collective memory theory and the existing literature on organizational anticipation, this study develops a novel theoretical framework positing that organizations simultaneously hold competing collective memories about sufficiency. These include memories of scarcity associated with recollections of hardship and deprivation, and memories of virtue linked to traditional wisdom and cultural heritage. Here, we contend that this dual-memory tension shapes organizations’ anticipatory capacity to imagine and implement sufficient futures. The paper elaborates on the concept of “organizational anticipatory capacity” and then presents a memory-anticipation matrix that employs Weberian ideal types to delineate how different configurations of collective memory types and anticipatory capabilities influence the adoption of sufficiency-oriented practices aimed at satisfying human needs within ecological boundaries. As such, it contributes to business ethics literature by theorizing the role of collective memory in promoting sufficiency-oriented transitions, and providing actionable pathways for building anticipatory capacity.
items.title: Between Scarcity and Virtue: How Collective Memory Shapes Organizational Capacity for Sufficiency Ethics

items.abstract: Abstract Recent social enterprise research has shifted attention from formal mission towards how ethics are enacted in everyday organisational practices, yet how institutional pressures reshape these practices at the frontline remains underexplored. Drawing on ethnographic research of a UK social enterprise operating under conditions of austerity and marketisation, this research explores how institutional pressures prompt organisational restructuring that gradually reshapes everyday caring practices leading to practice drift whilst the articulated social mission remains unchanged. Conceptualising social enterprise as a process of caring, we examine these changes across Tronto’s four phases of care. We identify frontline worker availability as a key foundation of relational care, showing how its locational, temporal and emotional dimensions can become decoupled, undermining the enactment of social mission. We also show how frontline workers’ moral distress in response to changing caring practices can provide an early indication of practice drift. This highlights the challenges that neoliberal institutional environments pose to social enterprises, and their ethical responsibility to sustain organisational policies and practices that enable frontline workers to enact the social mission.
items.title: Under Pressure: Frontline Worker Availability, Moral Distress and Practice Drift in Social Enterprise Through an Ethics of Care Perspective

items.abstract: Abstract In this work, I develop a novel mereotopology: a logic of the connection between objects or regions structured by mereological relations. The mereotopology here developed is explicitly guided by Descartes’ unique theories of surfaces. As I argue, Descartes’ philosophy has the requisite richness and depth to motivate a rigorous topological extension of mereology: an extension which rivals popular extant mereotopologies. The distinctive aspect of Descartes’ theory is that he takes boundaries to be modes of objects (or regions), rather than parts. To do justice to this key Cartesian choice-point, I cast the developed mereotopology in a higher-order logic. The axiomatization for this higher-order mereotopology is initially inspired by Descartes’ arguments, and several definitions and theorems are given based on this axiomatization. I conclude by discussing the philosophical merits of a Cartesian mereotopology. An appendix proves the consistency of this mereotopology, relative to ZF.
items.title: Cartesian mereotopology

items.abstract: Abstract A representation is considered accurate when its content matches the relevant elements of its object above a certain threshold. Philosophical views of accuracy conditions must therefore account for what determines the relevant elements, the threshold, and the object of a representation. These three features are crucial for theorizing about accuracy conditions of any representation, including memory representations. Recent literature on memory both in philosophy and psychology has typically addressed the determination of these features within a functional approach, assuming that they are determined by the functions of memory. This paper focuses on autobiographical memory, constituted of personal memories rich in phenomenological features, and examines how the functional approach accounts for its accuracy conditions. It begins by introducing autobiographical memory and the functional approach. It then discusses two families of functional hypotheses and their shortcomings before advancing a skeptical argument against the functional approach. Finally, it suggests that these features should instead be determined by pragmatic factors.
items.title: Against the functional approach to the accuracy conditions of autobiographical memories

items.abstract: Ethicists and activists often point to serious problems—e.g., global poverty, climate change, structural injustice, factory farming—and claim each of us has a duty to respond to them. This paper argues such expectations overlook the moral significance of specialization and division of labor among altruists. Extending Kant’s account of imperfect duty, I argue that conscientious altruists may focus their efforts on a limited set of causes and strategies while declining to participate in most others. I address concerns about how altruists should choose their specializations in the absence of market-like coordination mechanisms and respond to arguments that universal participation is required to mitigate complicity, address structural injustices, or avoid free riding. Although some limits on specialization exist, these typically leave individuals broad discretion over how they focus their efforts. The legitimacy and desirability of altruistic specialization should reshape the way we think about individuals’ responsibilities in a problem-filled world.
items.title: Altruistic specialization and division of labor

items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in natural language processing, but still struggle with complex logical reasoning. Previous work translates logical question-answering (QA) problems in natural language (NL) into a symbolic language (SL), and then employs an external logic solver to perform reasoning, in order to ensure the rigor and explainability of the inference. However, these neuro-symbolic methods usually rely on a fixed logic solver to handle all logical QA tasks, overlooking the selection of the most appropriate logic solver for each task. After categorizing logical QA tasks into two types—statement proving and satisfiability problems, we observe through experiments that solver performance varies across different logical QA tasks. To provide further explanation of our empirical observations, we theoretically compare three logic solvers—Prolog, Prover9, and Z3—in terms of languages and algorithms. Based on these empirical observations and theoretical analysis, we propose a hypothesis regarding the optimal match between logical QA tasks and logic solvers to improve the final performance of neuro-symbolic methods: proof-search-based solvers (such as Prover9) are optimal for statement proving problems, whereas satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers (such as Z3) excel at satisfiability problems. We validate our hypothesis by proposing a problem–solver matching method, adding an optimal solver matching stage before the NL-to-SL translation in typical neuro-symbolic methods. Experimental results on multiple logical QA benchmarks demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms single-solver baselines, achieving both performance improvements and better explainability.
items.title: Task-Matched Logic Solvers for LLMs: Toward Explainable AI

items.abstract: AI chatbots have become widespread across social, political, and commercial contexts, raising significant concerns about their potential to facilitate various forms of online harm. This systematic review synthesizes evidence on whether and how AI chatbots alter human judgment, memory, trust, and social behavior, and how those individual-level effects may scale into broader societal harms. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, a comprehensive search was conducted across six academic databases, applying predefined eligibility criteria to identify relevant studies published between 2020 and 2025. The findings show that ChatGPT and other OpenAI models represent the most extensively studied platforms in current research. The synthesized evidence shows that AI chatbots are associated with multiple forms of harm across technical, behavioral, and societal dimensions, including the spread of dis/misinformation, privacy violations, facilitation of cyberattacks, and enabling fraudulent activities. The results also show that only 7 of 71 studies applied explicit theoretical frameworks, suggesting that the field remains largely exploratory and descriptive. These findings can inform governance frameworks and risk mitigation strategies for addressing the challenges posed by AI chatbot technologies, though such interventions must be weighed against the demonstrated benefits of these tools in domains such as healthcare, education, and customer service.
items.title: The role of AI chatbots in facilitating online harm: a systematic review

items.abstract: Resistance to generative artificial intelligence is often dismissed as irrational, nostalgic, or futile. This article challenges that framing through an interpretive engagement with Chinese-language public discourse and media materials on everyday encounters with generated content. It identifies three interconnected forms of refusal. Quiet refusal appears when users immediately swipe away synthetic faces, voices, or prose. Protective refusal includes watermarking, adversarial cloaking, and other efforts to keep creative work from entering model-training pipelines without consent. Confrontational refusal emerges through community bans, public accusations, and livestreamed demonstrations in which artists are required to prove human authorship. To explain the embodied aversion that animates these practices, the article develops the concept of visceral refusal : the bodily rejection of generated content as an ethical response to questions of consent, provenance, labor, and simulated human interiority rather than as a bias to be corrected through design. The article specifies the normative conditions under which such aversion carries ethical weight, distinguishing it from mere distaste and from prejudice. It also introduces authenticity labor to describe the unpaid work of detecting synthetic content, documenting creative processes, and proving human authorship. Although these practices cannot stop the development of generative artificial intelligence, they remain consequential. They create economic and social friction, preserve the significance of human provenance, expose missing consent and verification infrastructures, and keep alternative technological arrangements imaginable. Refusal is therefore not merely opposition to technological change, but a generative ethical practice through which people defend their capacity to judge, distinguish, and withhold consent.
items.title: Visceral refusal: everyday resistance to generative AI in China

items.abstract: Abstract This is the introduction to the symposium ‘Fair profits and the law’, which starts from two main driving assumptions. The first is that there is structural shift in the current political economies that renders profit-making and fair profits again central categories and concerns – as they have been at various points in the history of capitalism. The second is that law and legal analysis can help make sense of this increasingly central phenomenon. But how exactly can they do that? The symposium is made up of ten papers drawn from a broad range of legal areas, and has three main goals in that respect. The first is to corroborate the emergence and consolidation of a right to profits and the specific form that such a right may take, on the one hand, and the countervailing efforts and techniques to limit or moderate claims to profits or to ensure their appropriate distribution, on the other hand. The second is to locate and legally contextualise the turn to profit-making, as discussions central to particular fields of law become discussions about guaranteeing profits or ensuring their fairness. The third is to explore whether, and the extent to which, the representation of profits and claims over them are organised through legal expertise, vis-à-vis the role of other competing logics and forms of expert knowledge.
items.title: Profit-making and fair profits: towards a new agenda for legal research

items.abstract: Abstract The transfer pricing regimes that apply to international corporate groups are meant to allocate corporate profits to the jurisdictions where the underlying value-creation takes place. But, owing to their market power, such groups can extract value created elsewhere in the global production network – hence the phenomenon of ‘residual’ profit not accounted for by arm’s length pricing of the group’s operations as between group members. The boundary of the corporate group therefore seemingly constitutes an obstacle to fair allocation of profits for global tax purposes, particularly where the source of that additional profit is independently owned low-wage production nodes in low-income countries whose margins are suppressed by the market power of lead firms. But relaxing that boundary does not tend to greater economic justice for the Global South/economic periphery because, on closer analysis, the obstacle is a deeper structural one: the fact that capital constituted into legal persons is enabled to cross borders into the Global South/economic periphery in order to exploit it commercially, but the polity among which that exploitation has taken place is not able to reach back across in the opposite direction to tax the proceeds of that exploitation.
items.title:
The fair allocation of profits between jurisdictions for tax purposes in a
                    monde compartimenté

items.abstract: Abstract Borderline Personality Disorder has been subject to important debate within feminism. It has been argued (Shaw and Proctor 2005) that BPD pathologizes women’s non-conforming behavior as a modern form of hysteria, serving misogynistic norms rather than alleviating psychological distress. Feminist critics have proposed different ways of addressing the problem: removing the diagnosis (Shaw and Proctor 2005), maintaining it but changing its meaning (Lester 2013), renaming it as c-PTSD (Herman 1992; Nicki 2016; Dorfman and Reynolds 2023) or recognizing some BPD features as traits of neurodivergence (Johnson 2021; Welch 2023). In this paper, we argue that the apparent conflict among feminist approaches stems from reified conception of mental disorder assumed in the discussions of BPD. In this sense, we argue that a constructivist non-reified view of mental disorder addresses the central claim of the different feminist proposals without their pitfalls. We present our constructivist view, expressivism , which lets us incorporate key feminist insights on BPD and supports a more nuanced view of the condition, focusing on identity and disability in mental suffering and pathology.
items.title: Borderline Personality Disorder and the Reification Problem

items.abstract: Abstract Since 1977, the World Health Organization (WHO) Model Lists of Essential Medicines (EML) have guided countries in selecting medicines that address priority health needs. This study explores how global and national stakeholders interpret the role of the WHO EML and why its impact on access varies across therapeutic areas. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 52 participants across 17 countries. Data were analyzed thematically and mapped onto a two-axis framework reflecting trust in EML as a selection reference and control over access policies. Findings reveal that the influence of the EML was greatest where inclusion aligned with financing and procurement mechanisms, as seen in HIV and hepatitis C, where pooled procurement and voluntary licensing (and compulsory licensing as in the case of hepatitis C medicines) translated listing into tangible access gains. In contrast, in high-priced therapeutic areas, EML inclusion was often described as aspirational, reflecting clinical priority without resolving affordability or implementation barriers. In many national settings, the EML substitutes for formal health technology assessment but remains weakly connected to reimbursement and procurement decisions. Overall, the study indicates that the influence of the WHO EML depends on whether its normative authority is linked to concrete mechanisms that enable affordability and access.
items.title: Global and National Perspectives on the Role of the WHO Model Lists of Essential Medicines

items.abstract: Abstract Drawing on the Confucian philosopher Mencius’s work, I develop a Mencian account of justice grounded in the virtue of yi (righteousness). Mencian justice grows out of xiuwu , a sense of shame and disdain for doing despicable things. The Mencian perspective posits that everyone possesses the innate capacity for a sense of shame, and the potential to expand one’s ethical selfhood in light of public standards of right. Yi enables citizens to firmly uphold what is right, refrain from doing what is unjust, and fight injustice. This novel account of Mencian justice rooted in the virtue of yi moves beyond existing Confucian accounts of distributive justice and ren (benevolence) based Mencian theories of moral cultivation. I show that this Mencian account is not merely of historical interest but also has contemporary relevance by exploring how yi might empower democratic citizens to confront environmental injustice.
items.title: Mencian Justice and Ecological Citizenship

items.abstract: Abstract Scholars have long recognized a gap in Aristotle’s Politics : he suggests leisure contributes to prudence, but he never explains what leisure contributes or how it does so. We argue that Churchill’s Painting as a Pastime helps fill this gap. To our knowledge, we are the first to situate Churchill’s understanding of leisure within the larger context of political philosophy. Churchill focuses on leisure’s ability to cultivate a “single unity of conception,” which trains the statesman to perceive and act upon the universal in the particular. Art educates prudence. By showing how leisure can nurture this ability, Churchill completes something omitted in Aristotle. Likewise, Churchill’s more Aristotelian approach shows why previous authors, such as Clausewitz, failed to connect this “unity of conception” to leisure. Leisure is essential to statesmanship, not just because it enriches life or consoles the politician, but because leisure alone trains the comprehensive vision necessary to political excellence.
items.title:
Churchill’s Theory of Leisure, Prudence, and Aristotle’s
                    Politics

items.abstract: In Lane’s thought-provoking book, painstaking attention to the different yet “interlocking” notions of rule and office—fused in the single word archē and its various forms in ancient Greek—foregrounds accountability as a primary problem for collective life. Lane’s rich readings of the Statesman, Republic , and Laws find his writing creatively tracking the question of how to keep rulers focused on “the good of the ruled” (19, 41). To clear the way for this line of inquiry, Lane must unsettle the common assumption that archē connotes exclusively a practice of absolute rule in Plato’s works. She persuasively does this by showing the reader how archē also connotes an additional sort, a subcategory, of ruling akin to officeholding. Over 11 chapters, Of Office and Rule makes clear that ignorance of or indifference to the polysemy of archē , at least in the officeholding sense, has made it difficult to enlist Plato’s thought as fully as we might want in thinking critically about the corruption afflicting any constitutional project.
items.title: Wages Not for Housework

items.abstract: In his magisterial study On Politics , Alan Ryan asserts that “Plato’s political thought is anti political.” 1 A related (if weaker) distinction has been championed by thinkers ranging from Du Bois to Arendt to Rancière to Wolin, opposing two kinds of politics: roughly, politics as hierarchical rule, versus politics as popular participation, struggle, and action. Before and in The Souls of Black Folk , for example, Du Bois adhered to what Robert Gooding-Williams calls “a Platonist picture of the rule of the thinking, knowledgeable few … over the benighted, ignorant many, who can socially integrate their lives by obeying the directives of their betters.” 2 Readers may therefore wonder what is new or distinctive in Of Rule and Office: Plato’s Ideas of the Political. 3 Does this work not simply reiterate the view of Plato as progenitor of hierarchical “rule,” as against a more participatory vision of politics?
items.title: Author’s Response: Rule and its Wages

items.abstract: Abstract Between 2000 and 2020, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) grew considerably, with operating expenditure more than doubling and the number of staff worldwide increasing from just over 10,000 to nearly 20,000. Concurrently, the institutional mandate of the ICRC expanded into new issue-areas. Examining three areas of ICRC mandate expansion—linked to protracted conflicts, other situations of violence beyond armed conflict, and responding to migration—this article asks how the modus operandi of the ICRC changed, and what this implies for its commitment to principled humanitarian action. It argues that, in each of these three issue-areas, working at the margins of international humanitarian law (IHL) has led the ICRC to undertake activities that are not compatible with its institutional commitment to neutrality. In making these arguments, the article contributes to our understanding of the work of the ICRC in the twenty-first century and sheds light on the important but usually obscured relationship between IHL and ICRC neutrality.
items.title: The ICRC and the Principle of Neutrality at the Margins of IHL

items.abstract: Abstract I argue that Sidgwick’s views on central ethical questions – the dualism of practical reason, the foundation of common sense morality – when combined with his epistemology, force him to ethical nihilism. Yet it would not have been difficult for him to avoid this conclusion by dropping one of his epistemological principles. Making this move on his behalf brings into focus not the alleged dualism of practical reason, but the more fundamental idea of three methods . The idea that ethics flows from three distinct intuitive sources, often in tension but never in contradiction, all of them valid, emerges as the great insight of the Methods of Ethics . So understood, Sidgwick offers a comprehensive approach to ethics and practical reason that is never over-simple or one-sided.
items.title: Sidgwick’s Nihilism

items.abstract: Julia Kristeva’s Melanie Klein , translated from the French by Ross Guberman, is a rewarding if at times difficult book that maps the pioneering contributions of Melanie Klein (1882–1960) to the field of psychoanalysis. The book proves challenging, especially in its more technical chapters, given Kristeva’s easy fluency with Klein’s often complicated theories and idiosyncratic practices. It will be most accessible to persons intimately familiar with Kleinian object-relations theory or others who, like Kristeva herself, have formal training in psychoanalysis. Yet Kristeva does facilitate the reader’s reception of Klein’s work by focusing not only on the innovative, imaginative ways in which the latter challenges psychoanalytic orthodoxies, but by explaining Klein’s relevance to today’s political landscape with its themes of alienation, xenophobia, techno-capitalist dominance and authoritarianism. Thus the text explores not only therapeutic topics pertinent to the analytic setting, but also the social and political import of these topics to the world today. This makes the book less exclusive to fellow psychoanalysts and more open to a general reading public. Moreover, Kristeva’s tendency to call the psychoanalyst ‘Melanie’ adds a note of endearment to what might otherwise be an intellectual struggle.
items.title: Melanie Klein

items.abstract: We often speak of exercising our rights. This article interrogates what is meant by this and considers implications for rights about the exercise of rights. It argues that what is meant by the exercise of a right differs according to whether we are speaking of a Hohfeldian claim‐right, liberty, power or immunity. Clarifying the exercisability (or not) of the different right relations is shown to have implications for our understanding of ‘equitable property’ rights on the important rights about rights model. When what is meant by the exercise of the different rights is borne in mind, it emerges that only the power can be held subject to a duty not to exercise it and that a duty not to exercise a liberty is a paradox. From this insight, it is argued that at least one ‘equitable property’ right – the restrictive covenant – is not a right about a right. It is suggested that this helps to account for its different third‐party effect.
items.title: Rights About the Exercise of Rights
